title: Locking away a held-out period
objectives: Reserve an out-of-sample period and use it exactly once.
Split the data with a purging gap and enforce a single look in code.

screens.title: What would you bet on?
screens.prose: All course we have tried rules on all five years of `make_bars()`. Here are the net Sharpe ratios of eight lookbacks over those five years, at 2.5 bp a trade. You would trade the best one, lookback 2.
screens.question: What Sharpe should you expect from lookback 2 over the next year?

options.text: 0.37, the number in the table
options.why: You picked lookback 2 because it scored highest on these five years. A number used to choose is biased up as a forecast.

options.text: Probably less than 0.37, and these five years cannot say how much less
More than 0.37, because more data will sharpen the edge
options.why: Nothing in the table grows with time. The next year is new noise around whatever the true edge is.

options.text: Nothing at all: a backtest says nothing about the future
options.why: That throws away too much. Data kept apart from the choosing can still give an honest estimate.

hints.text: Why is lookback 2 the one you are looking at?
It is the highest of eight numbers computed on the same data.
The highest of several noisy numbers tends to sit above its own true value. So the forecast should be lower, by an amount this data cannot measure.

feedback.correct: The data that chose the rule cannot also grade it.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Think about how lookback 2 came to be the one in front of you.

byKey.same: You took the winning number at face value. It won partly by luck, on the same data.

explain.text: You chose lookback 2 because it topped eight scores on the same five years. Some of its 0.37 is luck that will not repeat. To measure how much, we need data the choosing never touched.

screens.title: Lock the last year away
screens.prose: We fix this before any research. The last 252 bars, 14 November 2022 to 31 October 2023, are split off and locked away. Research may use only the bars before them. Slide the research window as far as it goes.
screens.question: How many bars can research use?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. The held-out year is the last 252 of 1,260 bars.

byKey.all: That includes the locked year. Research stops where the shading starts.

screens.title: Where the split goes
screens.prose: A colleague suggests a different held-out set: 252 days picked at random from the five years. That way every market condition is represented.
screens.question: Which held-out set gives an honest test of a trading rule?

options.text: The last 252 bars, as shaded
252 days picked at random
options.why: Random days sit between research days. A 2-day lookback reads its neighbours, so research and test share information (validation, shuffling lies).

options.text: The first 252 bars
options.why: Then research comes after the test. A rule chosen with later data has seen what happened next, which no trader can.

options.text: Any of them: 252 days is 252 days
options.why: The count matches, but the order matters. Only the end of the data is truly after everything research saw.

hints.text: When will the rule actually trade?
A rule trades after it is chosen, on days later than all its research.
The test should copy that: put the held-out year after every research bar.

feedback.correct: The test comes after everything that chose the rule.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask which set sits after all the research in time.

explain.text: You kept the test at the end, as a real launch would be. Random days leak through neighbouring bars, and an early test lets the future choose the rule.

screens.title: How much can one year say?
screens.prose: From l9: a Sharpe ratio measured over $T$ years has standard error about $\sqrt{(1 + SR^2/2)/T}$ (Lo, 2002). Suppose lookback 2's true net Sharpe really is its research value, 0.55, and we test it on one year.
screens.question: What is the standard error of the one-year Sharpe? Give 2 decimal places.

hints.text: Put $SR = 0.55$ and $T = 1$ into the formula.

feedback.correct: About 1.07: as large as the edge itself, twice over.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Use $T = 1$, for one year.

byKey.noroot: You stopped at $1.151$. Take the square root.
byKey.four: That uses $T = 4$, the research years. The test is one year.

explain.text: One year has a standard error of 1.07. Even if the edge were real at 0.55, the held-out year would come out below zero about 30% of the time. The held-out year is a sanity check that can catch a large error, not proof of a small edge.

screens.title: A gap between the two
screens.prose: Another rule holds each position for 20 days. Its last research trades are scored on bars inside the held-out year, so the two periods would share bars. We drop a gap of 20 bars before the held-out year (validation, purging).
screens.question: With `n_holdout = 252` and `gap = 20`, how many bars does research keep?

hints.text: The held-out year stays the last 252 bars.
The gap is cut from the end of research, just before the held-out year.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Keep the held-out year whole and take the gap from research.

byKey.nogap: That leaves no gap, so the 20-day trades still reach into the held-out year.
byKey.fromheld: You cut the gap from the held-out year. Keep the test whole and shorten research.
byKey.added: The gap removes bars. Research gets shorter, not longer.

explain.text: You took 20 bars off the end of research, leaving 988. No research trade can now be scored on a held-out bar. The gap should be as long as the rule's reach: its holding period or label horizon.

screens.title: Looking twice
screens.prose: You open the held-out year once. Lookback 2 makes a net Sharpe of −0.45 there. Lookback 10 made 1.86 in the same year, so you switch to it and report 1.86 as the held-out result.
screens.question: What is the 1.86 worth?

options.text: A held-out result: the year was opened only once
options.why: You opened it once, but you chose lookback 10 because of what you saw there.

options.text: An in-sample number: the year helped choose the rule, so it is research now
Half as reliable as a first look
options.why: There is no partial credit. Once a number guides a choice, it is a research number.

options.text: More reliable than −0.45, since it used more information
options.why: It used the test to choose, which is exactly what makes it unfit to test.

hints.text: Why did lookback 10 replace lookback 2?
Look at lookback 10's research Sharpe.
Lookback 10 lost money in research, −0.33. It was chosen only for its held-out score, so that score now did the choosing.

feedback.correct: The held-out year has become research.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask what chose lookback 10.

byKey.held: You counted opens, not choices. The 1.86 picked the rule, so it cannot grade it.
byKey.better: More information about the test year is the problem, not the cure.

explain.text: Lookback 10 lost money in research and won only in the test year, and you chose it for that. The year is now in-sample. An honest new estimate needs new data: paper trading from today.

screens.title: Split in code
screens.prose: Now the split as the engine's first step. `make_bars` and `BARS = make_bars()` are defined. Return the research frame and the held-out frame, with `gap` rows dropped between them.
screens.question: Complete `split_holdout(bars, n_holdout=252, gap=0)`.

widget.starter:
def split_holdout(bars, n_holdout=252, gap=0):
    # research: everything before the gap; held_out: the last n_holdout rows
    n = len(bars)
    research = ...
    held_out = ...
    return research, held_out
widget.solution:
def split_holdout(bars, n_holdout=252, gap=0):
    # research: everything before the gap; held_out: the last n_holdout rows
    n = len(bars)
    research = bars.iloc[: n - n_holdout - gap]
    held_out = bars.iloc[n - n_holdout:]
    return research, held_out
widget.how: Check runs 9 hidden tests: the lengths, the first and last dates as ISO strings, a gap of 20, a 10-row frame, and that no date is in both parts. Exact comparisons. The first run loads NumPy and pandas, which takes about 15 seconds; later runs are quick.

hints.text: Both parts are slices with `iloc`.
The held-out part is always the last `n_holdout` rows.
`research = bars.iloc[: n - n_holdout - gap]` and `held_out = bars.iloc[n - n_holdout:]`.

feedback.correct: The split runs before anything else touches the data.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Keep the last `n_holdout` rows whole and cut the gap from research.

explain.text: Slicing by position keeps the order of time. The gap comes off the end of research, so the held-out year is always the same 252 bars, whatever the gap.

screens.title: A vault that opens once
screens.prose: Discipline is easier when the code enforces it. A `Vault` holds the held-out data. Its `open()` returns the data the first time and raises `RuntimeError` on every later call. A new vault opens again. Note the last two tests: the data may be `None`.

lines: RuntimeError: the held-out data has already been opened
params.title: Expected

screens.question: Complete the `Vault` class.

widget.how: Check runs 7 hidden tests: a first open returns the same frame, every later open raises RuntimeError, a second vault is independent, and data that is None still counts as opened. The first run loads NumPy and pandas, which takes about 15 seconds; later runs are quick.

hints.text: The vault needs to remember one thing besides the data.
A flag such as `self._opened`, set to False in `__init__`.
In `open`, raise if the flag is set; otherwise set it and return `self._data`. Do not test the data itself, since it may be None.

feedback.correct: The second look now fails loudly.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Keep a flag apart from the data, and check the flag, not the data.

explain.text: The flag is separate from the data, so a vault holding `None` still locks. A raised error is better than a promise: the second look in a notebook now stops the run instead of quietly happening.

screens.title: Research, then one test
screens.prose: The whole protocol in one function. Defined already: `split_holdout`, `Vault`, and `net_sharpe(bars, lookback, cost_bp)`, which runs the course's engine (signal, targets, next-open fills, costs in bp) and returns the annualised net Sharpe. `LB` is the eight lookbacks and `TWIN` is `make_bars(phi=0.0)`.
screens.question: Complete `research_then_test(bars, lookbacks, cost_bp)`.

widget.how: Check runs 6 hidden tests on BARS and TWIN, with one, two, three and eight lookbacks, and one that counts how many times a vault was opened (it must be once). Tuples compared exactly after rounding to 3 places, expected values from this browser's pandas. The first run loads NumPy and pandas, which takes about 15 seconds; later runs are quick.

hints.text: Score every lookback on `research`, never on `held_out`.
`best = max(lookbacks, key=lambda L: scores[L])`.
Then `out = net_sharpe(vault.open(), best, cost_bp)`: the only time the held-out data is read.

feedback.correct: The protocol runs, and it tells the truth.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Choose on research only, then open the vault exactly once.

explain.text: On `make_bars()` research picks lookback 2 at 0.547, and the held-out year gives −0.453. Nothing is wrong with the code: that is the honest result, and it goes in the note under what failed.

screens.title: The rule you built
screens.prose:
What you built: the rule is chosen on research alone, $\theta^* = \arg\max_\theta SR(\theta;\ \text{research})$, and scored once on the vault, $SR(\theta^*;\ \text{held out})$. In code:

```python
research, held_out = split_holdout(bars, 252, gap)
vault = Vault(held_out)        # before any research
# ... choose rule, lookback, costs: research only ...
score = evaluate(vault.open(), frozen_settings)
```
screens.question: The held-out Sharpe disappoints. Which next step keeps the result honest?

options.text: Report it as it is, and test any new idea on data that does not exist yet: paper trading
Tweak the rule on research and open the year again
options.why: The year has been seen. Any change made after seeing it is guided by it.

options.text: Hold out a different year of the same five and test again
options.why: That year was in research. It helped choose the rule, so it cannot test it.

options.text: Leave the held-out result out of the note
options.why: Dropping the number that hurt is the one thing a reader can never check.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Which option uses data that played no part in any choice?

explain.text: After the vault is opened, all five years are in-sample. The only clean data left is what has not happened yet. A desk calls that paper trading, and it is the next test.

screens.title: Validated out of sample
screens.prose: A manager's deck says a strategy was "validated out of sample, Sharpe 1.4 in 2023". Due diligence learns that 2023 was the third year they tried as the test: the first two gave Sharpes below 0.3.
screens.question: What should the allocator take from the 1.4?

options.text: Little: three test years were tried and the best was shown, so 1.4 is a research number
It is a fair out-of-sample result for 2023
options.why: Each test year was out of sample once. Choosing which one to show turned all three into research.

options.text: The fair figure is the average, 0.63
options.why: Averaging is better than picking, but the rule was likely tuned between tries too. Ask for a period nobody has seen.

options.text: It proves the edge, since 2023 was a hard year
options.why: One year carries a standard error near 1, and this one was picked.

hints.text: How many times was a test year opened?
Three test years were tried; one was shown.
Showing the best of three tests is selection, the same as picking the best of three lookbacks.

feedback.correct: A test chosen from several is no longer a test.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count the looks, not the years.

explain.text: Three test years were opened and the best was shown. That is the trap from earlier on a manager's deck. An allocator asks for live or paper-traded months from after the deck was written.

ideas: The data that chooses a rule cannot also grade it: the best of several backtests is biased up.
Split off the last year before any research, leave a gap as long as the rule's reach, and open it once with every setting frozen.
One year has a Sharpe standard error near 1, so the held-out year is a sanity check, not proof.

formula.name: Held-out split
formula.tex: \underbrace{0, \dots, n - h - g - 1}_{\text{research}} \;\big|\; \underbrace{\cdots}_{g \text{ gap}} \;\big|\; \underbrace{n - h, \dots, n - 1}_{\text{held out}}
formula.note: Here $n = 1260$, $h = 252$: research is 1,008 bars with no gap.
